Lessons.Title: Exponent Review
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: review the meaning of whole-number exponents and distinguish exponentiation from repeated addition or multiplication of the exponent.
For a nonzero base a, a³ means a×a×a, not 3a. Zero exponent is defined as a⁰=1 for nonzero a, because it preserves the quotient pattern; zero to the zeroth power is not covered by that rule.
Represent powers using original square/cube diagrams and repeated-product notation. Teacher review checks whether the visual model correctly distinguishes base and exponent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Base
KeyConcepts.Definition: The number repeatedly multiplied.
KeyConcepts.Rule: In aⁿ, the base is a.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponent
KeyConcepts.Definition: How many factors of the base are multiplied for positive integer n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero exponent
KeyConcepts.Definition: Any nonzero base to power zero equals one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Square negative number
WorkedExamples.Question: Find (−3)².
WorkedExamples.Check: The square of a real number is nonnegative.

WorkedExamples.Title: Zero power
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 7⁰.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use exponent rule for nonzero base.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not generalize to 0⁰ without defining a convention.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An exponent counts repeated factors, not addition.
−3² means −(3²), unlike (−3)².
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify what exactly is raised to the power.

SummaryPoints: Nonzero bases to power zero equal one.

Lessons.Title: Multiplying Powers of Ten
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: discover and use the product rule for powers of ten by combining repeated factors and representing place-value shifts.
Multiplying 10ᵃ and 10ᵇ joins groups of factors of ten, giving 10ᵃ⁺ᵇ. The rule extends to signed integer exponents when a and b are integers, but this investigation first uses repeated products.
Draw a place-value table for 10²×10³ and explain why the outcome is 10⁵. A teacher checks mathematical pattern reasoning and table alignment.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/2/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Power product rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Same-base powers multiply by adding exponents.

KeyConcepts.Title: Place-value shift
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplication by 10 moves digits one place left in base ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Matching bases
KeyConcepts.Definition: The simple sum rule requires the same base.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The product rule uses addition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write expanded factors to see why.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying same-base law to different bases.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Common base condition matters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rewrite with common bases only when valid.

Visuals.Title: Multiply powers of ten
Visuals.Description: Original exponent evaluation table. The nonzero base is 10; negative powers mean reciprocals, never a logarithm approximation.

Lessons.Title: Powers of Powers of 10
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: reason about repeated multiplication of a power and derive the power-of-power rule (10ᵃ)ᵇ=10ᵃᵇ.
When (10²)³ appears, three copies of 10² are multiplied, giving 10²×10²×10²=10⁶. This differs from adding the exponents 2+3, which would give 10⁵.
Make an original exponent-tree representation grouping factors into equal blocks. Teacher review checks the explanation of grouping versus product.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/3/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Power of a power
KeyConcepts.Definition: An exponent outside parentheses counts copies of the inside power.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product contrast
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying same-base powers adds exponents.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expanded blocks
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each inner power contributes its own factor count.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Three copies of two factors give six.

WorkedExamples.Title: Power of power
WorkedExamples.Question: Simplify (10²)³.
Steps: The inside contains two factors of ten.
Repeat that block three times, for six factors.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding exponents in a power of a power.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Grouping repeats the inner factors multiplicatively.
10^(2³) is different from (10²)³.

Lessons.Title: Dividing Powers of 10
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: derive division of same-base powers by canceling equal nonzero factors and interpret exponents smaller than, equal to, or greater than the denominator exponent.
For powers of 10, 10ᵃ/10ᵇ=10ᵃ⁻ᵇ. When exponent difference is zero, the quotient equals one; when negative, the result is a reciprocal fraction. Division by zero is never allowed.
Draw factor-cancellation rows to explain 10⁵/10², then explore 10²/10⁵. A teacher assesses the cancellation model, while exact numeric answers are independently checkable.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/4/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quotient rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide powers of the same nonzero base by subtracting exponents.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cancel factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal nonzero factors in numerator and denominator cancel.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five factors over two leave three.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative exponent
KeyConcepts.Definition: A negative signed exponent represents a reciprocal power.

WorkedExamples.Title: Divide equal powers
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 10⁴/10⁴.
Steps: Any nonzero value divided by itself is 1.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both numerator and denominator are nonzero.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numerator exponent minus denominator exponent is the rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Concluding a smaller numerator gives zero.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A positive fraction can be below one without equal zero.

SummaryPoints: Equal nonzero powers divide to one.
Negative result exponent represents a reciprocal.

Visuals.Title: Divide powers of ten
Visuals.Description: Original exponent evaluation table. The nonzero base is 10; negative powers mean reciprocals, never a logarithm approximation.

Lessons.Title: Negative Exponents with Powers of 10
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use the exponent pattern to interpret negative powers of ten as positive rational reciprocals and convert them to decimal place values.
As exponent decreases by one, divide the value by ten. From 10⁰=1, it follows 10⁻¹=0.1 and 10⁻²=0.01. These values are not negative numbers; the sign belongs to the exponent.
Construct a place-value number line from 1 to 0.001 with labels. Teacher checks ordered spacing and explanation; a numerical conversion alone does not validate the drawn model.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/5/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative power
KeyConcepts.Definition: A reciprocal power of a nonzero base.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decimal movement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing by ten shifts decimal places rightward in place-value naming.

KeyConcepts.Title: Value versus sign
KeyConcepts.Definition: A negative exponent does not make a positive base negative.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare values
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is larger, 10⁻² or 10⁻⁴?
WorkedExamples.Check: A more negative power of 10 is smaller in positive value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a negative claim
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner says 10⁻¹=−10. Is that valid?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a negative exponent as a negative number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The exponent sign encodes reciprocal.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding a tiny positive value to zero without explanation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Positive fractions remain nonzero.

SummaryPoints: Negative powers of 10 are small positive reciprocals.
Consecutive exponents differ by factors of ten.

Visuals.Title: Negative powers mean reciprocals
Visuals.Description: Original exponent evaluation table. The nonzero base is 10; negative powers mean reciprocals, never a logarithm approximation.

Lessons.Title: What about Other Bases?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: extend integer-exponent laws beyond powers of ten to nonzero positive or negative bases, preserving sign and nonzero denominator restrictions.

The product, quotient and power-of-power laws work for any nonzero base where all terms are defined. A negative base enclosed in parentheses changes sign according to exponent parity; an unparenthesized negative sign may not be part of the base.
Compare 2³×2⁻⁵ and (−2)³. Work exact rational results and discuss why any logarithm problem is unrelated to this Grade 8 objective. A teacher reviews laws and symbolic justification.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/6/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same-base product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine exponents when multiplying one base.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same-base quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract denominator exponent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative-base parity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Odd powers of a negative base are negative, even powers are positive.

WorkedExamples.Title: Power of negative base
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute (−2)³.
WorkedExamples.Check: Different from −2³ only because parentheses define base, though this odd case has same value.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dropping parentheses from a negative base.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It may change the operation order.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write (−a)ⁿ when negative is part of base.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying laws to a zero denominator.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Division by zero is undefined.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require a nonzero base for signed exponents.

SummaryPoints: Exponent laws extend to any nonzero base.
Signs depend on base and parity.

Visuals.Title: Positive and negative exponents of two
Visuals.Description: Original exponent evaluation table. The nonzero base is 2; negative powers mean reciprocals, never a logarithm approximation.

Lessons.Title: Practice with Rational Bases
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: apply integer-exponent rules to rational bases, including reciprocals and negative exponents, and simplify exact fractions.
For a nonzero fraction p/q, the negative power (p/q)⁻ⁿ=(q/p)ⁿ. A negative fraction raised to an even power yields a positive result, while odd powers remain negative.
Create a rational-base card sort showing two expressions with the same value, then justify without floating-point rounding. Teacher checks symbolic reasoning and equivalence.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/7/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rational base
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction p/q where q≠0.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Nonzero base additionally requires p≠0 for negative powers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reciprocal rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Negative exponent swaps numerator and denominator.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sign parity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Even powers of a negative fraction are positive.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cube a rational base
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute (3/2)³.
WorkedExamples.Check: Equivalent to 3.375 but exact fraction preferred.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Negating the fraction instead of taking reciprocal.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Negative exponent is not a minus sign outside.
Both factors are raised to the exponent.

SummaryPoints: Rational bases obey integer exponent rules.

Lessons.Title: Combining Bases
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: multiply and divide products with different bases when exponent laws justify combining same exponents, without inventing an invalid same-base rule.
If two different bases have the same exponent, aⁿbⁿ=(ab)ⁿ. Conversely, a^m b^n cannot generally combine by adding m+n unless bases are equal. Prime factorization can sometimes expose a common base.
Compare 2³×5³ with 2³×5². Create a reasoned equivalence chart. A teacher reviews the symbolic factor grouping.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/8/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same exponent product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different bases but equal exponent can combine within parentheses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different exponent caution
KeyConcepts.Definition: Unlike bases and exponents cannot combine directly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common base rewrite
KeyConcepts.Definition: Express composite bases as powers of one number.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: aᵐbⁿ cannot be combined with simple exponent addition.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Look for a genuine common base.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: (ab)ⁿ is not abⁿ.

SummaryPoints: Same exponents can combine bases multiplicatively.
Never apply either law without checking its hypotheses.

Lessons.Title: Describing Large and Small Numbers Using Powers of 10
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use powers of ten to express very large and very small quantities efficiently and compare orders of magnitude.
A number such as 50,000 can be written 5×10⁴. A small decimal like 0.0007 equals 7×10⁻⁴. The exponent describes place value, not a count of decimal digits after arbitrary rounding.
Arrange original length and mass measurements on a powers-of-ten place-value chart. A teacher reviews the representation and order-of-magnitude explanation.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/9/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Large-number power
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying by 10ⁿ shifts magnitude up n decimal places.

KeyConcepts.Title: Small-number power
KeyConcepts.Definition: Negative power scales down by reciprocal of 10ⁿ.

KeyConcepts.Title: Order of magnitude
KeyConcepts.Definition: Comparing powers of ten for scale.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Powers differ by factors 10 per exponent step.

WorkedExamples.Title: Write large quantity
WorkedExamples.Question: Convert 50,000 to a one-digit factor times a power of ten.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare scales
WorkedExamples.Question: What is 10⁶/10³?
WorkedExamples.Check: One million is 1000 times one thousand.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting exponent from number of digits alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Leading nonzero coefficient matters.
Negative exponent means reciprocal.

SummaryPoints: Powers of ten encode place value.
Negative powers express small positive scales.

Visuals.Title: Decimal and scientific notation
Visuals.Description: Scientific notation has a leading factor from 1 to below 10.

Lessons.Title: Representing Large Numbers on the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: place large numbers expressed in powers of ten on a scaled number line and justify each point’s relative position.

A number line with ticks at multiples of 10⁶ can locate 3×10⁶ exactly at the third such tick. A logarithmic axis would behave differently; do not silently switch between linear and logarithmic scales.
Draw a line from 0 to 5,000,000 with million-unit spacing; locate 2.5×10⁶ and explain its midpoint position. A teacher checks the scale and labeling.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/10/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear large-number scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal distances represent equal numerical increments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Between-tick placement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractional multiples sit proportionally between ticks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale consistency
KeyConcepts.Definition: Do not change tick value partway through an axis.
KeyConcepts.Rule: All equal spaces use the same amount.
KeyConcepts.Example: Each 1-cm tick gap can represent one million.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plot two million
WorkedExamples.Question: Where is 2×10⁶ on a million-increment number line?
Steps: Each tick gap equals one million.
Place it two gaps right of zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plot midpoint
WorkedExamples.Question: Where is 2.5×10⁶ relative to 2×10⁶ and 3×10⁶?
WorkedExamples.Answer: Halfway between two and three million.
WorkedExamples.Check: Equal distance from both bounding values.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using equal spacing for powers 10²,10³,10⁴ on a linear number line.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The values are multiplicative, not equal additive steps.
Large coordinates become visually ambiguous.

SummaryPoints: Large powers can be located on linear scales.
Fractions of a tick gap encode intermediate values.

Lessons.Title: Representing Small Numbers on the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: position small positive decimals and negative powers of ten using correct fractional tick spacing, recognizing closeness to zero but not equality with zero.
A line from 0 to 0.001 marked every 0.0001 has ten equal intervals. 3×10⁻⁴ occupies the third positive tick; the negative coordinate −3×10⁻⁴ is three equal ticks left of zero on a signed line.
Create an original micro-distance axis and compare 0.0002,0.0005 and 0.0008. Teacher review checks the precision and regular spacing.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/11/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Small decimal location
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive decimal lies right of zero even if tiny.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tick interval
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal steps can represent a fixed fraction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If each tick is 10⁻⁴, third tick is 3×10⁻⁴.

KeyConcepts.Title: Signed small value
KeyConcepts.Definition: A negative decimal lies left of zero.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Its distance from zero equals its absolute value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Third positive tick
WorkedExamples.Question: If intervals are 0.0001, what is third tick right of zero?

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare small numbers
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is larger, 0.0002 or 0.0005?
WorkedExamples.Check: It lies farther right of zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Locate a negative decimal
WorkedExamples.Question: Where does −0.0003 lie on tick spacing 0.0001?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding all tiny values to zero.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A nonzero value remains distinguishable on an adequate scale.
Negative is left on ordinary increasing x-axis.

SummaryPoints: Small powers of ten can be graphed precisely.

Lessons.Title: Applications of Arithmetic with Powers of 10
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use exponent arithmetic to estimate and compute quantities spanning large and small scales, with appropriate units and reasonableness checks.

When multiplying a large and a small power, add signed exponents. When dividing measurements, subtract exponents. Decimal coefficients must also be multiplied or divided, and physical units must be handled separately.
Model the area of a microsensor rectangle of dimensions 3×10⁻³ m and 2×10⁻² m; find area and explain why the product exponent is −5. Teacher checks dimensional interpretation.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/12/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Add signed powers of ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coefficient product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply coefficients separately from powers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit consistency
KeyConcepts.Definition: Product of lengths gives area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Micro-area
WorkedExamples.Question: Rectangle length 3×10⁻³ m, width 2×10⁻² m. What area?

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Exponent law only combines powers, not coefficient arithmetic.
A product of two lengths is area.

SummaryPoints: Powers of ten simplify extreme-scale arithmetic.

Lessons.Title: Definition of Scientific Notation
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use normalized scientific notation a×10ⁿ with 1≤|a|<10 for nonzero quantities and integer n, retaining correct sign and magnitude.
The coefficient must have an absolute value at least one and less than ten. For 62000, 6.2×10⁴ is normalized; 62×10³ has the same value but is not in standard normalized form.
Write measurements from an original chart into normalized notation. Teacher checks decimal-place reasoning and units, not just pattern memorization.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/13/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Normalized coefficient
KeyConcepts.Definition: A real coefficient whose magnitude lies in [1,10).

KeyConcepts.Title: Integer ten-exponent
KeyConcepts.Definition: An integer power tracks decimal scaling.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative number
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sign remains with coefficient.

WorkedExamples.Title: Large number
WorkedExamples.Question: Write 62000 in scientific notation.
Steps: 62000→6.2 by moving decimal four positions left.

WorkedExamples.Title: Normalize expression
WorkedExamples.Question: Rewrite 45×10³ in standard notation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Move factor of ten into exponent.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Its absolute value is not below 10.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing the sign of a negative quantity during normalization.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Exponent changes magnitude, not original sign.

SummaryPoints: Convert both very large and very small numbers.

Visuals.Title: Scientific notation of 62,000
Visuals.Description: 62000=6.2×10⁴ after moving the decimal four places.

Lessons.Title: Multiplying, Dividing, and Estimating with Scientific Notation
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation, normalize results, and estimate their magnitude before calculating.
Multiply coefficients while adding exponent powers; divide coefficients while subtracting exponents. Re-normalize if the coefficient falls outside [1,10). Check for a zero denominator.
Compare original contexts of microscopic cell length and astronomical distance without claiming the same measurement units. Teacher reviews the interpretation and order-of-magnitude estimate.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/14/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scientific product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply coefficients and add powers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scientific quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide coefficients and subtract powers, denominator nonzero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Normalization
KeyConcepts.Definition: If |coefficient|≥10, shift one ten into exponent.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The coefficient is at least ten.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Shift decimal one place and increase exponent.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing exponents instead of subtracting them.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Powers of same base use quotient law.

SummaryPoints: Scientific notation simplifies extreme-scale products and quotients.

Lessons.Title: Adding and Subtracting with Scientific Notation
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: add or subtract scientific-notation quantities by aligning powers of ten before combining coefficients, avoiding invalid exponent combination.
Addition does not add exponents: 3×10⁵+2×10⁵=5×10⁵, but if exponents differ, first rewrite one with the other power. The quantities must have compatible units.
Create a place-value chart aligning 2.4×10⁶ and 3.0×10⁵; explain why 0.3×10⁶ is equal to the second term. A teacher checks representation and unit consistency.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/15/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common exponent
KeyConcepts.Definition: A shared ten-power factor before addition.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponent alignment
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rewrite a term with a chosen power.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit requirement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Only add quantities with compatible dimensions.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Exponent addition is multiplication law, not sum law.
The resulting number lacks meaning.

SummaryPoints: Align ten-powers before adding or subtracting.

Visuals.Title: Add like powers of ten
Visuals.Description: Both terms have scale 10⁵, so add coefficients: 3+2=5.

Lessons.Title: Is a Smartphone Smart Enough to Go to the Moon?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: apply scientific notation to compare hypothetical data storage, computing or transmission scales in a clearly defined technology scenario, stating assumptions and units.

A byte count and bit count differ by a factor of eight. Storage capacity and processing speed are different dimensions and cannot be compared as if both were the same quantity; a realistic moon mission also has reliability, power and radiation requirements beyond raw capacity.

Original hypothetical scenario: device A stores 1.2×10¹¹ bytes, device B stores 3×10¹⁰ bytes. Compare capacity and express device A in bits. Teacher reviews modeling limitations, evidence sources and why capacity alone does not establish flight suitability.

First-party Edulytiks adaptation informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/7/16/preparation.html . No publisher illustrations or assessments are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Byte conversion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Eight bits make one byte in the usual digital-data representation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ratio of capacities
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare measurements in the same unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple engineering constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: Mission readiness cannot be inferred from storage alone.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Consider fault tolerance, radiation, power and software.
KeyConcepts.Example: More bytes does not prove moon-flight suitability.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare capacities
WorkedExamples.Question: A has 1.2×10¹¹ bytes and B has 3×10¹⁰ bytes. Ratio?

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert to bits
WorkedExamples.Question: A has 1.2×10¹¹ bytes. How many bits?
WorkedExamples.Check: Bits and bytes are distinct units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate larger total
WorkedExamples.Question: Three devices each have capacity 1.2×10¹¹ bytes. Total?
WorkedExamples.Check: This is just capacity, not proven mission reliability.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing bit counts directly with byte counts.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Units differ by eightfold.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a consumer device is flight-qualified because storage is large.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Environmental and reliability requirements are separate.

SummaryPoints: Scientific notation supports digital scale comparisons.
Capacity is not sufficient to certify mission suitability.
